newsitem.title: UK: VLCC CHARTERING RATES REMAIN HIGH, FOCUS ON ASIA.
newsitem.headline: VLCC CHARTERING RATES REMAIN HIGH, FOCUS ON ASIA.

text.p: Chartering rates for 250,000 tonne Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) were still high by the week's end and the focus remained firmly on eastwards voyages from the Middle East, shipbrokers said.
While Mideast/West voyages were pegged at W65, Asian voyages were at a steamy W75 for Singapore and were still estimated up in the W85s for Japan.

"The limited list of August VLCCs remaining unfixed might suggest that rates could creep up a shade more for east and west destinations next week, although just how many more cargoes there might be for August loading will probably be concerning a few of the older ladies who have not yet been asked to dance," shipbrokers Galbraith's said in a weekly report.

Oil traders see an increasing tendency for U.S. oil refiners to buy shorter-haul crudes. The inauguration a month ago of Colombia's Ocensa pipeline marked a significant shift in the supply balance for U.S. buyers closer to home.
The Ocensa pipeline now carries roughly 450,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Colombian crudes into the Caribbean and this is expected to rise to over 600,000 bpd by the end of the year.
Iraqi crude oil exports under a U.N. oil-for-food deal appear imminent and the U.N. said it expected agreement on Baghdad's aid distribution plan early next week, allowing sales to resume.

Iraq may need to squeeze out two million bpd in order to reach a cash target by an early September deadline but analysts said the country's export capacity may be limited to 1.3 million. Exports are to emerge from Ceyhan and Mina al Bakr.
Brokers said Bayoil had already fixed the 337,000 tonne Concordia 1 on subjects for four days to load Iraqi crude from the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
Rates elsewhere were little changed. Aframax tankers moving across the Med were talked at around W110 while million-barrel vessels were talked closer to W77.5-80.
Cross-North Sea routes for 80,000 tonners were pegged at around W90-95 while 130,000 tonne Suezmaxes stood around five points higher.
West African fixing was very limited. The 130,000 tonne Knock Clune was chartered at W77.50 to the U.S. Gulf and this was seen broadly in line with assessments.
